headline: New moon springs flush the cut — fluke and first bonito show at Moriches Inlet
subhead: Bay water pushing 78 degrees has shoved the fluke out to the channels, and the incoming tide at the inlet mouth is turning up something new.
body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what bay water does in the first week of July — it cooked. Great South Bay pushed to 78.8°F on the flats and shallow guts, and that's too warm for a fluke that wants to sit still and ambush. What happened is predictable if you've watched this inlet long enough: the fluke abandoned the bay-side structure — the flats off Tuthill Point, the deeper holes inside Pattersquash — and ran for the channels and the inlet itself, where the exchange keeps things livable. Meanwhile the ocean side has been getting fed by upwelled water sitting around 71°F, a solid ten-degree gap from the bay. That thermal differential is doing the work for you right now. Any time you've got a 71-degree ocean stacked against 78-degree bay water, the inlet becomes a funnel, and everything that wants to breathe easier is going to stage right in that cut.

This week the moon tips the scales further. We're building into new moon springs, peaking around July 11-13 — bigger tidal range, faster water through the inlet, more exchange volume moving in and out on every cycle. For an inlet system like this one, spring tides aren't just about height, they're about velocity. Moriches Inlet has never had a stable throat — it's shifted meaningfully since the last few nor'easters reworked the bar — and right now the main channel is running deeper on the east side of the cut, closer to the Cupsogue side than it was two summers ago. Bigger tidal push through a narrower, deeper slot means the current lanes get more defined, the eddies behind the jetty rocks get more pronounced, and bait gets funneled harder than it does on neap water. That's good news if you're a fish that eats things in a current, and it's good news for you if you know where the seams are.

Fluke fishing has been a mixed bag but with real teeth to it when you find the right water. Best results have come working the deeper cut just inside the inlet on the last two hours of the outgoing, dragging 3/4-ounce white bucktails tipped with 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets along the bottom where the channel drops from eight feet to fourteen off the Cupsogue side. Guys working the ocean-side rip just outside the jetties on the same stage have done better on bigger fish — 4 to 6 pounds mixed in with the schoolies — using a high-low rig with squid strips and a chunk of spearing, fished slow on the drift in 15 to 20 feet. The bay-side bite inside Moriches proper has gone quiet during the heat of midday; if you're fishing there, mornings on the last of the incoming are your window before the sun pushes surface temps too high for the fluke to commit.

Striped bass have been intermittent but not absent. The real window has been the last hour of outgoing into the first hour of dead low, right at the throat of the inlet where the current compresses and any bass staging there gets a crack at whatever's getting swept through. Bucktails with a white or chartreuse Gulp trailer worked slow along bottom, and swimming plugs — SP Minnows and Bombers in bone or bunker patterns — worked the surface eddies behind the rocks at Cupsogue after dark, have both produced. Nothing huge — most fish in the 24 to 30 inch range — but consistent enough that two or three fish a tide isn't a bad night if you're putting in the time on the right stage.

The story I'm most interested in this week is what showed up on the ocean side in the last few days — the first Spanish mackerel and bonito reports of the season working the clean incoming water outside the inlet. This is right on schedule. The pelagic watch window that's been building since the Fourth is closing out over the next day or two, and Moriches and Shinnecock ocean-side water have both produced. If you've got a light spinning rod and some small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks or Kastmasters in silver — this is the moment to run out to the ocean side on a clean incoming tide and work the surface just outside the bar. These fish don't stick around long and they don't tolerate dirty water, so you want the tide as clear as it gets, which on this system means right after the last of a strong outgoing has scoured the inlet mouth.

Weakfish have been a non-story so far this year in this system, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. Water temp alone isn't the trigger people hoped it would be — we've had warm water for weeks now with nothing to show for it in this bay. If they show, it'll likely be an incidental catch working bucktails for bass at the inlet mouth rather than a targeted fishery.

Looking ahead: if the springs build the way they're set up to, I'd expect the inlet current to sharpen through the weekend, which should concentrate both the fluke and the bass tighter into the main channel and the rip just outside the jetties. That's where I'd spend my time — working the outgoing at Cupsogue for fluke, then switching to bucktails and plugs at last light for bass as the tide slacks. Keep an eye on the ocean side for those mackerel and bonito showing again on the next clean incoming — that window's closing, but it's not closed yet.
